765.bp: When data flows through a machine learning pipeline—preprocessed, cleaned, trained on—nobody can verify which actual data was used or if those records stayed true over time. Practitioners and regulators need to know: what specific data went into this model? Was it tampered with? Did it come from where we think it did? This matters for auditing, legal compliance, and trust.
765.wh: Most transparency tools describe *what* a model does (its predictions) or *why* it made a decision (its reasoning), but they don't track *how* individual data samples physically move through the pipeline. Without that trail, you can't tell if a sample was switched, duplicated, or removed after the fact. Current systems operate at the model level, not the sample level.

FG-Trac adds a tamper-proof record to every step: as data gets preprocessed, trained, and checkpointed, the system captures and cryptographically anchors each event. Rather than redesigning the model, it sits alongside it and records exactly what happened to each piece of data and when, creating an auditable chain of evidence.
765.ww: Cryptographic commitments (mathematical fingerprints) let you prove that records haven't been altered after the fact. By recording contribution scores tied to training snapshots, the system proves not just that data was used, but how much it mattered. This works without retraining anything because it operates purely on the data and metadata flow, not the model internals.
765.po: Teams can now produce verifiable proof that specific samples were processed correctly, show regulators a complete history of data usage, and detect tampering. The framework runs with low overhead and works on real pipelines (tested on both image and graph learning tasks) while keeping model performance intact.

766.bp: When you have access to multiple AI models—cheap but slow, fast but expensive, general-purpose or specialized—routing each question to the right one (instead of always using the biggest) saves money while keeping quality high. This is the core challenge of LLM serving: with a limited budget and varying types of incoming questions, how do you pick which model to use for each one?
766.wh: The obvious approach—always use the best model—blows the budget. But greedily picking the cheapest model tanks quality. The hard part is that you don't know in advance how good a model's answer will be for a particular question, and the mix of questions keeps changing. You need to adapt in real time without tuning knobs manually.
766.ap: BARouter watches each incoming query and estimates how good each available model would be, weighs that against its cost, and checks how much budget has been spent so far. Then it picks the model that best balances quality and cost given the remaining budget. It does this online—no retraining, just updating decisions query by query.
766.ww: The framework treats this as a sequential decision problem: each choice learns from past choices to get better. By keeping track of how much quality you gained per dollar spent and staying within budget, the system naturally learns which models work best for which kinds of questions. The math guarantees that this approach eventually finds nearly-optimal routing without manual tuning.
766.po: Models get routed efficiently: the right query hits the right model at the right time. Systems can work with different budgets and handle shifts in what questions come in, automatically staying robust without needing engineers to retune parameters. Theory proves the algorithm achieves near-optimal regret (minimal wasted budget and quality loss).

767.bp: Short videos (TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube Shorts) spread false information faster and wider than any other format. The speed and reach make it urgent to detect which videos are faked, AI-generated, taken out of context, or designed to exploit human biases—and then explain *why* each one is false so people can understand the deception.
767.wh: Most benchmarks test only one type of fake (say, just AI-generated deepfakes), but real misinformation mixes multiple tricks: an AI voice, real-but-recontextualized footage, and audio that plays on fears. Worse, existing detectors don't explain *how* they spotted the fake—they just say yes or no. Without explanation, people don't believe the verdict.
767.ap: WildFakeBench is a dataset of 10,000+ real videos labeled by experts with *what type* of manipulation happened. FakeAgent is a multi-agent reasoning system (inspired by the Delphi method of collecting expert views) that looks at each video frame-by-frame, extracts sound, searches for related news and context online, and then reasons through what it finds. Different agents specialize in different tricks: one checks for AI patterns, one for out-of-context reuse, one for cognitive bias.
767.ww: By having specialized reasoning agents compare the video against external evidence, the system catches tricks that would fool a single monolithic detector. Searching online reveals if this footage appeared somewhere legitimate first, or if the audio is from a known voice generator. Multiple agents seeing different red flags builds a stronger case than one model trying to learn all patterns at once.
767.po: The benchmark gives researchers a realistic, diverse test set with real-world videos and expert labels. The agent system outperforms existing LLM approaches on all misinformation types and explains *why* each video is fake—what manipulation was spotted and what evidence proved it. This makes debunking practical: people don't just get told a video is false, they see the reasoning.

768.bp: When you ask an LLM to find and use knowledge from documents—pulling relevant paragraphs to answer your question—the model only sees the raw text chunks it retrieves. But real understanding often comes from *connecting* ideas across chunks: how does this fact relate to that principle? Where are the gaps? The real goal is to retrieve emergent understanding, not just overlapping text.
768.wh: Current graph-based approaches try two things: (1) link concepts logically and retrieve related ideas, or (2) keep text context intact by chunking smartly. But both search for similarity within their original fragments. They miss the insight that springs from *synthesis*—connecting two separate ideas creates a third insight that exists nowhere in the source.
768.ap: HyGRAG builds a multi-level graph: chunks and entities live side-by-side in a hierarchy. The system clusters these together, has the LLM write summaries that fuse chunk context *and* entity relationships, then searches through all levels at once. When retrieving, it finds related ideas by following entity groups, expanding across different abstraction layers, and updates dynamically when documents change.
768.ww: Hierarchical search lets you start broad (what concepts matter?) and zoom in (what text explains this concept?) or start specific and link up to larger themes. Summaries written by the LLM at each cluster level capture *what that group means as a whole*, not just what text matched. This lets the retriever find synthesized understanding rather than just text overlap.
768.po: Queries retrieve more relevant knowledge across document hierarchies, revealing connections that chunk-based retrieval would miss. The system handles changing corpora efficiently—adding new documents only requires local re-summarization, not full rebuilding. This bridges the gap between entity-centric precision and chunk-centric context.

769.bp: In federated learning, many organizations train a shared model together without sharing raw data—each keeps data local. If someone later demands that their data be forgotten (right to deletion, poisoning recovery), the system must remove that person's influence from the global model. But this unlearning process creates a new risk: attackers might steal the deleted data by analyzing gradient updates.
769.wh: Unlearning requires either retraining everything or rolling back checkpoints, both expensive. Adding privacy protection (differential privacy) makes it even more costly because you need to add noise to gradients. The tension: protect privacy of removed data (use privacy budget), maintain model accuracy (also uses privacy budget), and keep computations fast. You can't maximize all three.
769.ap: DIARY intelligently splits the privacy budget between training and recovery phases based on what matters most for each. It also introduces FIND, an anomaly detector that runs during recovery to catch poisoned gradients. If anomalies appear, the system uses a two-level storage system to roll back to a safer checkpoint and reruns recovery. This reduces noise and avoids wasteful recomputation.
769.ww: By recognizing that different phases have different privacy needs, DIARY uses the total privacy budget more effectively. The anomaly detection catches attacks early, so you don't waste privacy budget protecting against something you've already identified and mitigated. The rollback mechanism means you only re-run the expensive parts when truly necessary.
769.po: The framework removes a client's data influence while defending against gradient inversion (where attackers try to reverse-engineer the deleted data from updates). It uses privacy budget efficiently across training and recovery, reduces computational overhead through smart rollback, and is proven secure against both poisoning attacks and privacy attacks that target federated unlearning systems.

770.bp: Clickbait headlines—'You won't believe what happened next!'—trick people into clicking false or exaggerated stories. An LLM could help detect this, but LLMs tend to agree with what users seem to believe or want to hear. The goal: use that flaw strategically to generate diverse perspectives on a headline, then combine them to spot clickbait robustly.
770.wh: LLMs naturally mirror the assumptions in your prompt. If a headline sounds sensational, the LLM might accept that framing instead of questioning it. Most detection systems rely on labeled training data (scarce for clickbait) or fine-tuning (expensive). How do you get diverse reasoning without ground truth or manual labels?
770.ap: SORG prompts an LLM twice on the same headline: once to argue it's credible, once to argue it's misleading. The model's sycophancy tendency now helps—it generates opposing arguments as if genuinely convinced of each side. These pairs become training signal. Then a smaller, local model (BERT-based) learns to evaluate headlines using these synthetically generated arguments as soft guidance and contrast learning (training on pairs of opposing views).
770.ww: By generating both 'agree' and 'disagree' reasoning, you get diverse perspectives without needing labeled data. The soft labels from the LLM's credibility scores guide the smaller model to recognize when reasoning is defensive (sign of clickbait) versus evidential. Contrast learning makes the detector learn which linguistic patterns signal credibility versus exaggeration by comparing reasoned arguments side-by-side.
770.po: The method detects clickbait without needing hand-labeled examples, outperforms pure LLM prompting and fine-tuned smaller models. It works by extracting implicit reasoning from the LLM's sycophancy rather than fighting it, then grounding detection in generated reasoning pairs and soft credibility scores.

771.bp: YouTube's recommendation system shows billions of videos daily. Users can click buttons like 'Not Interested' or 'Don't Recommend Channel,' intending to filter what they see. But do these controls actually work? If they don't, users lose agency and get stuck in recommendation cycles. Trust in the platform erodes.
771.wh: Testing whether these buttons work requires immense scale: each user sees thousands of videos, but unwanted recommendations are rare. You can't tell if a control worked by checking a handful of users or days of data. You need a measurement system large enough to detect small effects and randomization to prove causation, not correlation.
771.ap: Researchers built a browser extension and recruited 22,000+ users over six months, generating 567 million recommendations. A button overlaid each video; depending on random assignment, clicking it triggered different feedback signals (Dislike, Not Interested, Don't Recommend Channel, Remove from History, or nothing as control). They then measured whether similar videos reappeared afterward, using machine learning to estimate video similarity.
771.ww: Randomization lets you compare: for users who click 'Not Interested,' does unwanted content disappear faster than for the control group? Large sample size catches small effects that single-user tests would miss. By training a model to detect video similarity, they could count *how many* similar recommendations snuck back through, not just if any appeared.
771.po: The audit reveals YouTube's controls are largely ineffective—even the strongest barely prevented half of similar recommendations. This documents a concrete gap between user expectations and platform behavior, grounding platform accountability in empirical measurement. The findings suggest designers and policymakers need to rethink recommendation control architecture.

772.bp: Imagine a centralized platform (e.g., a hospital scheduler) making decisions for many users (departments) while keeping each user's identity hidden. The platform needs to assign resources fairly based on individual preferences, but it must not reveal who wanted what. Anonymity is essential when decisions are sensitive.
772.wh: Standard decision-making algorithms either break anonymity (they track which user prefers which arm) or give up on optimality (they treat everyone the same). Adding anonymity constraints makes the problem harder: the decision-maker must assign options without leaving traces of individual preferences.
772.ap: The algorithm uses successive elimination (a bandit technique that narrows down good arms by testing them repeatedly) to map which users prefer which options, building a multi-graph structure. Then it applies greedy matching (assigning arms to users like a bipartite matching problem) to allocate fairly. All of this happens without recording which specific user wanted which arm.
772.ww: Successive elimination works well for discovery because it doesn't need to track individuals—only which arms were tested and how often. Greedy matching separates the discovery phase (which arms are good) from the allocation phase (who gets what), allowing anonymity to be preserved at the allocation layer while still learning efficiently.
772.po: The framework achieves anonymity while solving the assignment problem optimally (up to a small factor in regret). Users get fair, personalized decisions; the platform learns which options are good; but no one—not even the decision-maker—learns which specific user prefers which arm.

773.bp: Text-to-speech and voice conversion technologies can now synthesize speech so realistic that humans struggle to tell real from fake. Synthetic voices pose security risks: someone could impersonate another person and trick contacts into sending money or revealing secrets. Detecting deepfake audio is urgent and difficult.
773.wh: Self-supervised models trained on large audio corpora learn useful representations at many layers: early layers catch low-level artifacts (digital glitches), later layers catch semantic patterns. But existing detectors treat each layer independently. They ignore that synthetic artifacts often *propagate* across layers—a glitch early on distorts patterns downstream. Temporal sequences within frames matter too.
773.ap: HierCon models the dependencies *between* layers: it learns which layers matter for detecting which types of fakes and how information flows across them. It also models temporal patterns: attention mechanisms that look at frame sequences, not frame-by-frame. The learning is grounded in margin-based contrast—training the detector to separate real and synthetic embeddings with a learned margin.
773.ww: Hierarchical modeling captures that artifacts in synthetic speech are not isolated layer-by-layer—they're systematic patterns that span the representation hierarchy. By learning to attend across layers and time, the detector picks up on these systematic distortions. Margin-based contrast makes the learned representations robust across different speech synthesis techniques and recording conditions.
773.po: Detection accuracy improves significantly: 36.6% and 22.5% error reduction on two benchmark datasets. The method generalizes to unseen synthesis techniques and real-world recordings. Attention visualizations show the framework learned to look at the right layer combinations for different types of deepfakes.

774.bp: AI agents now browse websites and make purchases, book flights, or transfer money on behalf of users. But a user granting an agent access to their bank account is dangerous: the agent might be tricked into authorizing the wrong transfer. How do you let agents do critical tasks while giving users fine-grained control over what the agent can do?
774.wh: Websites were designed for human interaction: you enter your password once, then do many actions. AI agents need to make many sequential decisions, but you can't ask the user to approve every action—that defeats the point of delegation. Standard authorization systems (OAuth, for example) give all-or-nothing access: either the agent can do everything or nothing.
774.ap: The paper proposes designing websites with built-in access control for agents: certain actions (like viewing balance) might not need approval, while others (like transfers over a threshold) do. The agent follows authorized steps without human intervention on low-risk actions, but the system blocks high-risk ones or asks for explicit approval. This requires modifying both website design and the authorization protocols.
774.ww: By distinguishing risk levels—some agent actions are safe by default (viewing public info), others need approval (spending money, deleting data)—you reduce approval burden while maintaining safety. Clear protocols mean the agent knows in advance what it can and cannot do, avoiding failures mid-task.
774.po: Agents can delegate tasks like bill payments to users without requiring approval for every keystroke, yet users retain control over critical actions. The framework demonstrates that access-controlled websites for agentic AI are technically feasible and usable.

775.bp: Imagine billions of AI agents (from different companies, with different goals) discovering each other, contracting with each other, and coordinating on tasks—all without a central authority. This is the agentic web. For it to work at scale, agents need to find each other (registry), trust each other (reputation), and agree on value (pricing). The internet's early foundations (DNS, HTTP) answered these for humans; what do we need for agents?
775.wh: Agents are not humans: they don't read natural language contracts or negotiate in real time. They need machine-readable standards, formal protocols, and incentive mechanisms built in. Decentralized identity, pricing, and reputation are hard unsolved problems when you can't trust a central authority.
775.ap: The tutorial outlines NANDA—three layers. *Foundations* (discovery, identity, protocols): agents need ways to find and authenticate each other, like DNS for agents. *Agentic Economy* (pricing, reputation, markets): agents trade services and build trust through transparent transaction histories. *Agentic Society* (governance, coordination): as populations of agents emerge, norms and incentives keep them aligned without central control.
775.ww: By treating the agentic web as having distinct layers (each solved separately but building on lower layers), you can design the infrastructure incrementally. Reputation systems naturally emerge from transaction history. Pricing and markets let agents converge on what services are worth. Identity and discovery are prerequisites for everything else.
775.po: The tutorial provides a conceptual framework for understanding what infrastructure the agentic web needs and why—grounded in lessons from the human web's evolution. It highlights open research challenges and positions next steps for building safe, scalable systems where autonomous agents coordinate at scale.

776.bp: Adversarial prompts can trick powerful language models into generating harmful content by carefully rewording requests or embedding hidden instructions. Defenses typically scan prompts for keywords or fine-tune the model, but these are slow and evasion-prone. You need a fast, lightweight defense that lives inside the model without slowing it down.
776.wh: Most defenses happen before the model generates (checking the prompt) or after (filtering outputs), both expensive. Modifying the model itself requires retraining. The hard part: finding internal signals that distinguish jailbreaks from legitimate requests quickly, without changing the model or incurring high latency.
776.ap: PADD prepends a harmless safety prefix to each prompt and measures how attention patterns shift between the original and prefixed versions. Jailbreaks typically use adversarial phrasing designed to manipulate attention in specific ways; harmless requests don't trigger these shifts. The detector compares attention distributions and plasticity (how responsive attention is), flagging high divergence as likely jailbreaks.
776.ww: Adversarial prompts and safe prompts affect the model's attention mechanisms differently—harmful instructions trigger attention patterns that bypass safety, while normal requests don't. By comparing against a prefixed version (a kind of control), the system isolates the effect of the adversarial content itself without needing to modify weights or fine-tune.
776.po: The defense blocks 96.7-99.6% of jailbreaks across multiple models while rejecting very few legitimate requests (0-5.2% false positive rate). Because it runs in a single forward pass, latency is low. No model modification or fine-tuning is needed—it works immediately on existing LLMs.

777.bp: Language models claim certainty even when they're guessing. They don't recognize knowledge gaps or conflicts in their training data. For reliable AI systems, you need the model to introspect—assessing its own uncertainty, spotting contradictions, and knowing when to slow down and think carefully instead of rushing to an answer.
777.wh: A single LLM can't reliably assess its own confidence. Multiple models (an ensemble) see different things, but they need to coordinate: which models are reliable for this question? When should the system take time to deliberate instead of answering fast? How do you measure and act on self-awareness?
777.ap: The system computes a Metacognitive State Vector (MSV)—a five-dimensional score capturing emotional response, correctness judgment, experience matching, conflicting signals, and problem importance. Each ensemble member gets an MSV score. The system then routes simple queries to fast System 1 processing (quick answers) and complex ones to System 2 (careful deliberation with specialized roles: Domain Expert, Critic, Evaluator, Synthesizer). Role assignment is based on MSV states.
777.ww: By modeling five dimensions from cognitive psychology, the system captures the kind of self-awareness that humans use to decide when to think carefully. Routing based on MSV automatically dedicates computation to hard problems while letting easy ones run fast. Specialized roles in System 2 (Critic questions answers, Evaluator judges quality) ensure deliberation is structured.
777.po: The proof-of-concept demonstrates that LLM ensembles can introspect meaningfully, routing queries appropriately and executing deliberation with different role assignments for different question types. Users can see how query complexity triggers System 1 vs. System 2 modes.

778.bp: Finding similar items in large databases powers recommendations, search, and personalization. The standard setup: you have a single reference (a query) and search for neighbors. But real applications need more: 'Find products similar to *all* of these favorites' or 'Find items similar to *any* of these interests.' Multi-reference search is more useful but unsupported by existing methods.
778.wh: Existing approximate nearest neighbor algorithms are built for single-reference queries. Extending them naively—searching separately for each reference and intersecting results—is slow. You need a unified approach that can score items based on their combined similarity to multiple references and execute efficiently on existing graph indexes.
778.ap: The paper defines new distance metrics: for all-k queries (similar to *all* references), score items by their minimum distance to any reference; for any-k queries (similar to *any* reference), score by minimum distance. Then it shows how to search these metrics on standard ANN graph indexes by adapting the traversal strategy. A two-stage search variant improves performance further.
778.ww: By defining clear distance metrics first, the problem becomes: how do you search for items matching these metrics on existing indexes? The key insight is that graph traversal can be adapted—starting from multiple entry points and following different rules—to find items matching the all/any-k criteria without rebuilding the index.
778.po: Applications can now query for multi-reference similarities efficiently: 'Show me products liked by all my family members' or 'recommendations matching any of these interests.' The method works on real-world datasets and outperforms baselines that solve the problem inefficiently.

779.bp: Misinformation thrives on social media because it's diverse, context-dependent, and exploits human psychology. A single detector can't catch all types. But multiple AI agents reasoning together, each spotting different red flags, can build a stronger case. The challenge: how do you coordinate multiple agents so they focus on what matters, not on the noise?
779.wh: When you feed agents all available information, they drown in truthful content and miss weak deceptive signals. Most multi-agent systems treat all information equally or let dominant patterns overwhelm subtle cues. Agents need to specialize and communicate without amplifying bias—easier said than done.
779.ap: PAMAS organizes agents into three levels. *Auditors* examine specific feature subsets (images, audio, text sentiment) and flag anomalies. *Coordinators* aggregate their findings while maintaining diversity—combining perspectives without letting one strong signal drown out others. *Decision-Maker* has full context and evolving memory, synthesizing all auditor insights into a verdict. The system also optimizes agent topology and routing dynamically.
779.ww: By giving agents specialized views and aggregating hierarchically (auditors spot anomalies in their domain, coordinators combine without bias, decision-maker synthesizes), the system avoids information drowning. Auditors working on feature subsets naturally surface weak deceptive cues that a full-context agent would miss. Memory helps the decision-maker learn patterns over time.
779.po: The multi-agent framework detects misinformation more robustly than single-agent approaches, explaining its reasoning through visible anomaly cues and specialized evidence. Dynamic routing and topology optimization reduce communication overhead, making multi-agent misinformation detection practical for real-time deployment.
